paras: The Beach's Still dance shooting took place on the night of February 7, 1903, when two white men fired into a Black dance near Beach's Still and McDonald in Coffee County, Georgia, killing two turpentine workers, Sam Bell and Aleck Mervin, and wounding nine or more others. The attackers reportedly tied survivors to the dead and robbed them, and though they were said to be locally known, a coroner's jury blamed "unknown parties" and no arrest was reported. Georgia papers and the Black Savannah Tribune condemned the inaction, and Governor Terrell offered a $250 reward per killer.

Beach's Still lay on the south side of Coffee County, about twenty-two miles from Waycross, where the first reports were filed. The first wire added that several "riots" between Black and white residents had occurred there in the previous ten years. The dead men were turpentine hands at a nearby still, and the festival was held at a Black guest's house.

About 11 o'clock on Saturday night, while the dance was under way, two white men appeared at the two doors of the house and began firing into the crowd. The first wire mentioned "a little difficulty" beforehand, but later Waycross reports said the men fired without warning on an "unusually peaceable" gathering. At least twenty-five shots were fired as the dancers struggled toward the one window; three women were among the wounded.

When most had fled, the men tied several wounded to the bodies of the dead and robbed the dead and living of money and weapons. Returning later, they cut the ropes and threatened to kill the survivors if they ever named the shooters.

A justice of the peace held an inquest Sunday afternoon; the jury found the men "came to their death by gun shot wounds from the hands of unknown parties." Sheriff Southerland went from Douglas to McDonald on Monday and returned without making an arrest. Waycross dispatches said the shooters were known, had been drunk, and were armed and "desperate," while Black witnesses would not talk for fear of being killed.

On February 26, on an affidavit from Solicitor General John Bennett, Governor Terrell offered $250 for each killer, above the usual $150, alongside a reward in the mob killing of Will Fambro in Spalding County. The Fitzgerald Enterprise complained on February 27 that no warrant had been sworn out, and no report of an arrest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached national readers on February 9 as a Waycross wire about a "riot" between two white men and "a crowd of negroes," under headlines such as "Negro Riot in Georgia" and "Georgia Race Trouble." A Macon Telegraph version calling it a "race riot" at McDonald was still running in western weeklies on February 12. Some editors rejected the label: the Salt Lake Herald headed the wire "Cold-Blooded Murder," and the Washington Evening Star said "it looks very much as if the colored men lost the race."

The Savannah Morning News followed the case for weeks, heading one report "Murderers at Large in Coffee County" and writing that local indignation was "no less because the victims were negroes." The Americus Times-Recorder described a "reign of terror" by "white desperadoes," and the Fitzgerald Enterprise called the "Beach's Still outrage" "Coffee's shame." The Birmingham Age-Herald filed the case under "Lynching in Georgia" and dismissed the rewards as "grandstand plays."

The only Black-press item found, a February 14 Savannah Tribune paragraph, cited the killings as proof of "much lawlessness in Coffee County" and said a sheriff afraid to do his duty should be replaced. Where white editors appealed to the county's good name, the Tribune ended: "But it is only Negroes that are concerned and of them it makes no difference."

Accounts placed the shooting at Beach's Still, at McDonald, or two miles from McDonald's mill, and the Telegraph dated it Sunday rather than Saturday night. Counts of the wounded ranged from nine, in the wire and the affidavit, to "not less than twelve" in later Waycross reports; none recorded a third death. Later local reports set aside the wire's hint of a quarrel, calling the shooting unprovoked and done "almost solely for the purpose of robbery."

reader.title: Beach's Still dance shooting
bases: Two armed white men fired into a Black dance from its doorways, killing two and wounding others, then bound and robbed survivors; no accusation against the victims and no custody seizure was reported (A1, A22, A26).

The Waycross wire, a separate Macon Telegraph special, later Waycross and Douglas correspondence, and the solicitor general's affidavit all report two white men shooting into a Black dance in Coffee County, killing two (A1, A10, A17, A22, A26).

accounts.gist: A 'race riot' at McDonald on Feb. 8 between two white men and a crowd of negroes; two killed, one mortally and eight badly wounded.

accounts.label: Later Waycross correspondence
accounts.gist: Unprovoked attack on a peaceable festival by two drunken white men, chiefly for robbery; at least twelve injured; survivors tied to the dead, robbed and threatened; shooters known but unarrested.

accounts.label: Solicitor general's affidavit
accounts.gist: Unknown white persons fired on a dance two miles from McDonald's mill on Feb. 7, killing Alex Mervin and Sambo Bell and wounding nine, then tied and robbed the dead and living.

accounts.label: Black editorial
accounts.gist: Two white men killed and wounded several colored persons; the murderers are well known but unarrested, and the sheriff should be replaced if afraid.

framing.detail: National papers ran the wire as a 'riot' or 'race riot' ('Negro Riot in Georgia', 'Georgia Race Trouble', 'Three Die in Race Riot').
The Salt Lake Herald headed the wire 'Cold-Blooded Murder'; the Washington Evening Star mocked the 'race riot' label.
Savannah Morning News, Americus Times-Recorder and Fitzgerald Enterprise called it murder by 'desperadoes', 'Coffee's shame', and demanded arrests.
Birmingham Age-Herald grouped it under 'Lynching in Georgia', called the attackers a mob, and called rewards 'grandstand plays'.
Savannah Tribune: 'much lawlessness in Coffee County'; the sheriff should be replaced; 'it is only Negroes that are concerned'.
